transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?
Hi, thanks for having me. Things are going well, thanks for asking. I've been busy with classes and my internship, but I'm excited to talk about the work I've done, so I'm glad to be here.
That's great. So what drew you to this kind of role, working in software engineering?

I think what got me hooked was the checkout project at my internship. I was working on a page that took about three seconds to load on mobile, which doesn't sound like much, but you can actually see customers giving up on it. Figuring out why it was slow, then watching it drop to about 1.8 seconds after I changed how the scripts loaded, made me realize I really like that kind of problem: something concrete, measurable, and that people use every day. That's the kind of work I want to keep doing.
Got it. So when you say you changed how the scripts loaded, what exactly did you do there?

So the page was loading three payment scripts right away, before anything else. I profiled it with Lighthouse and real-user timing to confirm that was the bottleneck. Then I deferred two of the scripts so they loaded after the page was usable, and lazy-loaded the card form so it only loaded when someone actually reached that step. Mobile load went from about 3.1 seconds to about 1.8.
That makes sense. Was that something you identified and did yourself, or did someone point you toward that approach?

My manager suggested I look at the scripts, so that was the starting direction. But I did the profiling myself to find which ones were the problem, and I made the actual changes to defer two scripts and lazy-load the card form. I'd say the pointer got me looking in the right place, and the rest of the work was mine.
Got it. Let's switch gears—tell me about a time you failed at something.

Early on with the TA job, I tried to explain loops the same way the textbook does, and one student just kept failing. I was getting frustrated, and honestly I think I was more focused on explaining it well than on figuring out where they were getting stuck. What helped was sitting down with them and drawing out the traces on paper, step by step, so they could see the variables change. It took about three weeks, but they passed the midterm, and I learned that I should slow down and watch someone work through a problem before I start explaining.
That's helpful. Did you change how you ran the labs after that, or was it just the way you worked with that one student?

Yeah, I did change some things after that. Before, I'd spend most of the lab time up front explaining the concept, then answer questions. Now I start by asking students to trace a small piece of code on paper, and I only step in once I see where they're getting stuck. I also started checking in with the students who were quiet, since they were usually the ones falling behind without saying anything. It's a small shift, but it made the labs a lot more useful, at least from what I could tell.
How'd you know the labs were actually more useful? Did you get feedback, or notice something specific change with the students?

Honestly, it was a mix of both, but I'll be upfront that I didn't run any formal survey. I asked students a few questions at the end of labs, like which part confused them most, and the answers got more specific. Instead of "I don't get loops," I'd hear "I can't tell when the counter changes." I also noticed fewer students waiting around with their hands up, and more of them were tracing code on their own before asking me. That's not hard data, so I'd call it a reasonable signal rather than proof.
Got it. When you noticed those things—the more specific questions and students tracing code on their own—did that change how you actually ran the labs after that?

Yeah, it did. Once I saw that students were asking more specific questions, I started building the first part of each lab around a short tracing exercise, so they'd hit the tricky parts early instead of waiting for me to explain everything. I also began asking the question I'd been asking at the end of labs at the start too, something like "where do you think the counter changes?", so I could catch confusion before it snowballed. The one thing I kept from the early mistake is that I try to hold back for a few minutes before jumping in, because the students usually get further on their own than I expect.
That makes sense. Do you remember a specific student where you saw that shift actually happen—like, someone who was really stuck at the start of the semester and then turned it around?

Yeah, I think about that one a lot. It was the student who kept failing the loop questions. I'd explain loops the way the textbook does, and it wasn't landing. Then we spent about three weeks sitting down together and drawing out the traces on paper, one step at a time, so they could see the variables change. By the midterm they passed, and that's when I really noticed the difference in how I was teaching.
That's helpful. So when you say they passed the midterm—do you know if that student ended up passing the class overall, or what their grade looked like by the end?

I don't actually know their final grade for the class. I was a TA, so I saw them in lab and during our sessions, but I didn't have access to the final grades, and I didn't follow up after the semester ended. What I can say is that they passed the midterm, which was the point where I could see the change most clearly. I'd be guessing if I said more than that.
Fair enough. Let's switch gears a bit. Looking at your resume, you've got the internship and the TA role both listed for summer 2026—how'd you manage both at the same time?

It was pretty manageable. The TA job was only about four hours a week, all remote, in the evenings, so it fit around the internship without much trouble. I kept my evenings for lab prep and grading, and I blocked off time on my calendar so the internship work during the day didn't get squeezed.
Got it. So let's talk about the work itself at the internship. You mentioned improving test coverage across the billing service—what was the coverage percentage before you started that work?

Before I started, coverage across the billing service was about 38%. It went up to about 61%. I should be clear about my part, though: I wrote the tests for the invoice proration module, which was about 40 tests, and two teammates handled the rest of the coverage work.
That's helpful context. So for those 40 tests you wrote—what was the coverage on the invoice proration module specifically before and after your work?

I don't have a number for the proration module on its own. The 38% to 61% figure is for the whole billing service, and I didn't pull a separate before and after for that one module. I know the 40 tests I wrote covered the proration logic, but I'd be making up a percentage if I gave you one now. If you want, I can say what the module covers and what kinds of cases the tests check.
That works. What kinds of cases did those 40 tests cover?

Mostly the edge cases where proration gets tricky. Things like a subscription starting or ending partway through a billing cycle, mid-cycle plan changes, and months with different day counts, since that's where the math tends to go wrong. I also wrote tests for zero-amount and rounding cases, so we didn't end up with off-by-a-cent invoices. I didn't keep a formal list of all 40, so I can't walk you through each one, but those were the main areas I focused on.
Got it. Let's switch to the payments dashboard you built in React. Who on the support team actually used it, and what were they doing before you built it?

Before the dashboard, the support team exported data from a spreadsheet every day, and that's what they used to look up refunds. The team is six people. The biggest change was refund lookups, which went from about five minutes each to under one minute. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API it pulls from, so I want to be clear that the backend wasn't mine.
What part of the React front end did you build yourself, versus what did someone else on the team handle?

I built the whole front end, so the screens the support team actually clicks through, the refund lookup flow, and how the data gets displayed. The senior engineer owned the API and the data it returns, so I was working against their endpoints. If something in the response wasn't shaped the way I needed, I'd go back and talk to them about it, but I didn't write or change the server code.
Got it. Let's switch gears. Tell me about a time you failed or something that didn't go the way you planned.

Honestly, the one that comes to mind is at Campus Eats. Users were double-tapping "Pay," and sometimes they got charged twice. I hadn't planned for that, and it was the hardest problem we ran into. I ended up adding idempotency keys to the ordering backend so a repeated request couldn't create a second charge. That fixed it, and it taught me to think about what happens when users do things I didn't expect.
How did you find out that was happening in the first place?

I don't remember the exact moment we caught it, and I'd be guessing if I gave you a specific story. What I can say is that it showed up as users reporting they'd been charged twice, and once we looked at the orders, we could see the duplicate payment requests coming from quick repeat taps on the Pay button. I was on the ordering backend, so I was the one digging into the request logs to confirm the pattern.
Got it. When you added the idempotency keys, did you write that code yourself, or was that a team decision on how to fix it?

Good question. I wrote the idempotency key code myself. The team agreed that the ordering backend needed to stop duplicate requests, and I was the one on the backend, so I implemented it. I did run the approach past my teammates before merging, since it touched how payments get processed, but the implementation was mine.
Thanks. Before you made that change, how many duplicate charges were actually happening—do you know the number?
